question: Which route accounts for most urinary tract infections?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the various routes by which bacteria enter the urinary tract and cause infection

options.text: Ascending spread through the urinary tract
options.rationale: Most urinary tract infections arise by ascending spread through the continuous urinary column from the urethra toward the bladder or kidneys.

options.text: Hematogenous spread through the renal circulation
options.rationale: Hematogenous spread is a rare route. It would be correct if organisms reached the kidneys through the bloodstream rather than ascending from below.

options.text: Direct spread across the renal capsule
options.rationale: Direct capsular spread is not the usual route described. It would require infection extending directly from tissue adjacent to the kidney.

options.text: Descending spread through the urinary tract
options.rationale: The typical direction is upward from the urethra, not downward from the kidneys. Descending involvement would require an infection originating at a higher urinary site.

options.text: Lymphatic spread into the renal parenchyma
options.rationale: Lymphatic spread is not identified as the predominant route. It would require entry through lymphatic channels rather than the urinary column.

question: A urine dipstick detects an enzyme released by white blood cells. Which test produced this result?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: The blood pad detects blood rather than an enzyme released by leukocytes. It would fit a specimen evaluated specifically for hematuria.
The glucose pad evaluates urinary glucose rather than pyuria. It would fit a specimen being assessed for glucosuria.
Leukocyte esterase is released by white blood cells, so its detection reflects pyuria and is used to identify more than 10 leukocytes per high-power field.
The nitrite test depends on bacterial conversion of nitrate to nitrite. It would fit screening for bacteriuria caused by nitrate-reducing gram-negative organisms.
The protein pad does not detect a leukocyte-derived enzyme. It would fit evaluation of urinary protein rather than pyuria.

question: Which organism causes the largest proportion of uncomplicated urinary tract infections?
cited_learning_objective: Know the most common organisms that cause UTIs

options.rationale: Proteus mirabilis accounts for only about 1-2% of uncomplicated infections. It would be more plausible if a less common gram-negative cause were sought.
Klebsiella species account for about 1-2% of uncomplicated infections. They would be more plausible in the broader organism distribution of complicated disease.
Enterococci cause approximately 1-2% of uncomplicated infections. They become more prominent among complicated infections.
Staphylococcus saprophyticus is an important cause but accounts for a smaller proportion than the leading organism. It would fit one of the two common causes of uncomplicated cystitis.
Escherichia coli is the dominant cause of uncomplicated urinary tract infection, accounting for approximately 70-95% of cases.

question: Which microscopic finding may occur when infection involves the upper urinary tract?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the spectrum of urinary tract infection (UTIs)

options.rationale: Red blood cells may be seen in urinary infection, but red blood cell casts are not the cast finding identified for upper urinary infection. This would require a different renal process.
White blood cell casts may be present in pyelonephritis and support involvement above the bladder.
Epithelial cell casts are not the urinary cast associated with pyelonephritis in the source material. They would require a different tubular process.
Granular casts are not the stated microscopy feature of pyelonephritis. A different renal parenchymal process would be needed.
Hyaline casts are not the identified marker of upper urinary infection. The relevant inflammatory finding is a cast containing white blood cells.

question: A symptomatic patient has a positive nitrite dipstick result. Which microbial function most directly produced this finding?
cited_learning_objective: Know the most common organisms that cause UTIs

options.rationale: This reverses the direction of the dipstick-relevant reaction. The finding requires production of nitrite from urinary nitrate.
Leukocyte esterase is released by white blood cells rather than bacteria. This would fit the leukocyte esterase pad only if inflammatory cells supplied the enzyme.
Bacteria do not produce the blood-pad result by releasing blood. Blood positivity would instead reflect blood present in the urine.
The nitrite screen relies on gram-negative bacteria converting urinary nitrate to nitrite, thereby providing evidence of bacteriuria.
Esterase is an enzyme released by leukocytes, not a substrate converted into leukocytes. Pyuria would instead produce a positive leukocyte esterase result.

question: A healthy woman has dysuria, frequency, and urgency without vaginal discharge, fever, back pain, or flank pain. Which diagnostic and treatment approach is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Obtain imaging before starting directed therapy
options.rationale: The presentation supports uncomplicated cystitis without a stated structural concern. Imaging would become relevant if an obstructive or structural abnormality were suspected.

options.text: Obtain microscopy before starting directed therapy
options.rationale: Microscopy can identify pyuria or bacteria but is not essential before treating typical uncomplicated cystitis. It would be more useful if the diagnosis were uncertain.

options.text: Obtain culture before starting directed therapy
options.rationale: Culture is not essential before treatment of typical uncomplicated cystitis. It would be required for suspected complicated infection or useful when therapy must be tailored.

options.text: Begin empiric therapy without mandatory testing
options.rationale: Typical uncomplicated cystitis is diagnosed clinically and treated empirically; urine culture and dipstick testing are not essential before treatment.

options.text: Delay therapy pending susceptibility test results
options.rationale: Waiting for susceptibility results is unnecessary in uncomplicated cystitis. This approach would fit an infection requiring culture-directed therapy.

question: A urine specimen contains 14 white blood cells per high-power field. Which interpretation is most accurate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: The specimen meets the threshold for pyuria
options.rationale: Pyuria is defined as more than 10 white blood cells per high-power field, so a count of 14 meets the stated threshold.

options.text: The specimen excludes inflammatory urinary disease
options.rationale: A count above 10 supports rather than excludes urinary inflammation. Exclusion would require a count below the stated pyuria threshold.

options.text: The specimen proves upper urinary infection
options.rationale: Pyuria supports urinary inflammation but does not by itself localize infection to the kidneys. Upper tract involvement would be supported by fever, flank pain, or white blood cell casts.
White blood cell quantity does not establish bacterial Gram classification. A positive nitrite result would more specifically support nitrate-reducing gram-negative bacteria.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria requires a positive urine culture without urinary symptoms. A white blood cell count alone does not establish that diagnosis.

question: Which feature converts an otherwise typical urinary infection into a complicated infection?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the differences between uncomplicated and complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs)

options.rationale: A prior infection is a risk factor but does not itself compromise the urinary tract or host defenses. Complication requires a structural, functional, or host-defense factor.
Female sex increases UTI risk but does not alone define a complicated infection. An otherwise healthy woman without urinary abnormalities can have uncomplicated disease.
Sexual activity is a risk factor for uncomplicated infection. It does not itself create an impaired urinary tract or compromised host defense.
Obesity appears among risk factors for uncomplicated infection but is not listed as a defining complicating condition. A structural or host-defense abnormality would change classification.
An indwelling catheter or other drainage device is a foreign body that compromises the urinary tract and therefore makes the infection complicated.

question: An infection is classified as complicated because of urinary retention. Which management principle distinguishes it from simple cystitis?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the differences between uncomplicated and complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs)

options.text: Treat briefly without obtaining culture results
options.rationale: Complicated infection requires culture and generally a longer course. Brief treatment without culture fits uncomplicated cystitis rather than infection with retention.

options.text: Treat symptoms without correcting urinary retention
options.rationale: Failure or recurrence is likely unless the underlying functional abnormality is corrected. This approach would be acceptable only if no correctable abnormality existed.

options.text: Obtain culture and tailor antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Every suspected complicated infection should be cultured, with antimicrobial therapy subsequently based on organism identification and susceptibility.

options.text: Avoid culture because resistance is uncommon
options.rationale: Complicated infections involve a wider organism range and higher drug-resistance rates. Avoiding culture would contradict the need for susceptibility-guided therapy.

options.text: Assume the same organism distribution always
options.rationale: Complicated infections have a broader causative-organism distribution than uncomplicated infections. A narrow assumption would fit neither their microbiology nor resistance risk.

question: A patient has fever, dysuria, urinary frequency, and flank pain. Urinalysis shows pyuria. Which additional test is required to guide possible modification of initial empiric treatment?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Blood may be present in UTI, but it does not identify the organism or determine antimicrobial susceptibility. It would be useful only for detecting hematuria.
A glucose dipstick does not identify the pathogen or guide antibiotic modification. It would be relevant to glucosuria rather than antimicrobial selection.
Leukocyte esterase supports pyuria but cannot identify the causative organism or its susceptibility. It would help screen for urinary inflammation.
Microscopy may demonstrate cells, bacteria, or casts but does not provide organism-level susceptibility results. It would help characterize urinary sediment.
Pyelonephritis evaluation includes urine culture, which confirms the organism and permits modification of empiric therapy based on susceptibility.

question: A catheter becomes colonized during prolonged use. Which factor most strongly determines whether bacteriuria develops?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Catheter duration is the major determinant because colonization progresses each day and biofilm ultimately develops on the indwelling device.
Drainage-bag position is an important care measure but is not the major determinant of bacteriuria. It would matter when evaluating maintenance practices.
Regular bag emptying is recommended but does not replace minimizing catheter duration. It would be relevant to appropriate catheter care.
Proper securing is preventive care but is not the principal determinant of bacteriuria. It would matter when assessing catheter maintenance.
Hand hygiene reduces preventable contamination, but duration remains the dominant determinant. Hand hygiene would be the key issue if contact-related contamination were being assessed.

question: A patient develops a urinary infection associated with an indwelling catheter. Which intervention directly removes a persistent nidus for reinfection?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Raise the drainage bag above bladder level
options.rationale: The drainage bag should remain below bladder level. Raising it neither removes biofilm nor follows appropriate catheter care.

options.text: Open the drainage system for ventilation
options.rationale: A closed drainage system should be maintained. Opening it increases opportunities for contamination without removing established biofilm.

options.text: Delay catheter care until therapy finishes
options.rationale: Leaving the colonized catheter in place preserves the biofilm nidus. Catheter intervention should accompany treatment rather than wait until completion.

options.text: Replace the urethral catheter during treatment
options.rationale: Changing the catheter removes biofilm that can serve as a nidus for reinfection while antimicrobial therapy treats the infection.

options.text: Disconnect the drainage tubing each day
options.rationale: Repeated disconnection disrupts the closed system and does not reliably eliminate catheter biofilm. It would increase manipulation, itself a risk factor.

question: A woman has three culture-confirmed urinary infections during one year. Each follows documented clearance of the preceding organism. Which recurrence pattern is present?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria lacks local and systemic urinary symptoms and is detected incidentally. This patient has separate culture-confirmed infections after clearance.
Catheter colonization requires an indwelling device and does not describe cleared episodes followed by new infections. It would fit persistent bacteriuria during catheter use.
Reinfection is recurrence with the same or a different organism after the prior organism has been cleared from the genitourinary tract.
Relapse occurs when the same organism was never cleared. It would fit repeated infection with persistence of the original organism.
A complicated infection requires a compromising urinary or host factor. Documented clearance between episodes instead supports reinfection.

question: A recurrent urinary infection repeatedly grows the same organism, and testing shows that it was never cleared. Which additional response is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Persistence of the same organism suggests relapse and may reflect an underlying lesion. Reassurance alone would fit uncomplicated reinfection after documented clearance.
Reinfection requires clearance before recurrence. Persistence of the same organism instead defines relapse.

options.text: Stop therapy after one asymptomatic day
options.rationale: Symptom improvement does not demonstrate organism clearance. Stopping early would not address the persistent focus.

options.text: Use symptom history without culture comparison
options.rationale: Distinguishing relapse from reinfection depends on organism identity and clearance. Symptoms alone cannot establish this distinction.

options.text: Consider evaluation for a structural lesion
options.rationale: Relapse with an uncleared organism may require urologic evaluation for a structural lesion that maintains the infectious reservoir.

question: Which prevention strategy is preferred for a woman with recognizable recurrent simple cystitis who can accurately identify her episodes?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Continuous prophylaxis is reserved for situations in which other strategies fail. It would become appropriate after less intensive approaches are unsuccessful.
Patient-initiated self-diagnosis and self-treatment is the preferred strategy for appropriate patients with recognizable recurrent cystitis.
Postcoital prophylaxis is an alternative when episodes are linked to intercourse. The preferred general strategy for a reliable self-diagnosing patient is patient-initiated treatment.
An indwelling catheter increases bacteriuria and infection risk. It would be used only for a separate necessary drainage indication.
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria does not prevent recurrent symptomatic infection and promotes adverse events and resistance. Treatment is reserved for specified high-risk groups.

question: A 26-year-old woman has dysuria and frequency for 2 days. She has no fever, back pain, flank pain, vaginal discharge, structural abnormality, or neurologic urinary dysfunction. Which management is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Obtain culture and await susceptibility results
options.rationale: This delays treatment of a clinically typical uncomplicated cystitis episode. Waiting for susceptibility results would be appropriate when culture-directed treatment is required.

options.text: Begin parenteral therapy for fourteen days
options.rationale: Parenteral 14-day therapy is used for overt pyelonephritis in pregnancy, not afebrile uncomplicated cystitis.
The absence of systemic or flank findings and complicating abnormalities supports uncomplicated cystitis, which is treated empirically without mandatory culture or dipstick testing.

options.text: Urgently decompress the upper urinary tract
options.rationale: Urgent decompression is required when infection coexists with obstruction. No obstructive feature is provided in this patient.
The patient has urinary symptoms, so this is not asymptomatic bacteriuria. Observation would fit an asymptomatic nonpregnant patient without a qualifying procedure.

question: A 31-year-old woman has dysuria, urgency, fever, and unilateral flank pain. Urinalysis shows 18 white blood cells per high-power field [0-5 per high-power field]. Which diagnostic step should accompany initial empiric therapy?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Obtain urine culture for susceptibility testing
options.rationale: Fever and flank pain with pyuria support pyelonephritis. Culture identifies the organism and permits modification of initial empiric treatment according to susceptibility.
Symptom-only treatment without culture is suitable for typical uncomplicated cystitis. Pyelonephritis requires urinalysis and urine culture.

options.text: Repeat the blood dipstick after treatment
options.rationale: A blood dipstick neither identifies the organism nor provides susceptibility data. It would only assess whether blood is present in urine.

options.text: Classify the illness as simple cystitis
options.rationale: Fever and flank pain indicate upper tract involvement rather than isolated bladder infection. Simple cystitis generally lacks these findings.
Pyelonephritis requires prompt empiric treatment, followed by modification if culture results warrant. Withholding treatment risks progression.

question: A 72-year-old man has fever, hypotension, flank pain, and an infected obstructed collecting system. He is too unstable for general anesthesia. Which next step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Antibiotics alone are inadequate when infected urine remains obstructed. This would fit an infection without obstruction or severe illness.
An infected obstructed system is a medical emergency requiring urgent restoration of urine flow. Delayed definitive intervention is acceptable only after initial decompression stabilizes the patient.
Stenting under general anesthesia is riskier in a severely ill patient. It may become appropriate as a definitive procedure after stabilization.
Percutaneous nephrostomy provides urgent decompression with mild sedation and local anesthesia, allowing antibiotics, hemodynamics, and renal function to improve.
Persistent obstruction permits infection to worsen and spread. Observation is inappropriate because obstruction with active infection is an emergency.

question: A 79-year-old catheterized patient develops otherwise unexplained fever and leukocytosis. Which method should be used to obtain a urine culture specimen?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Collect urine from the existing drainage bag
options.rationale: The existing system may contain colonizing organisms and biofilm. A fresh specimen should follow removal or replacement of the catheter.

options.text: Remove the catheter and collect midstream urine
options.rationale: For suspected catheter-associated infection, the catheter should first be removed, followed by collection of a midstream specimen or sampling through a newly placed catheter.

options.text: Culture material scraped from catheter biofilm
options.rationale: Biofilm culture would reflect catheter colonization rather than provide the recommended urine specimen. Biofilm is addressed by catheter replacement.

options.text: Collect urine after opening the drainage tubing
options.rationale: Opening the system violates closed drainage and introduces contamination. A specimen should instead come after removal or through a new catheter.

options.text: Delay culture until the catheter is unchanged
options.rationale: Leaving the colonized catheter unchanged preserves biofilm and compromises specimen quality. Catheter removal or replacement should precede collection.

question: A patient with a long-term urethral catheter is diagnosed with catheter-associated urinary infection. Culture and susceptibility results are available. Which combined management is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Culture-directed therapy while retaining the same catheter
options.rationale: Directed treatment addresses the organism but retaining the catheter leaves biofilm as a reinfection nidus. Catheter replacement should accompany therapy.

options.text: Empiric therapy while ignoring susceptibility results
options.rationale: Once susceptibility data are available, treatment should be selected from those results. Empiric selection is used only before definitive data are known.
Replacing the catheter removes biofilm but does not by itself treat an established symptomatic infection. Both source control and appropriate antimicrobials are needed.

options.text: Routine observation with daily drainage disconnection
options.rationale: Symptomatic catheter-associated infection requires treatment, and repeated disconnection disrupts the closed system. Observation alone fits neither the infection nor safe catheter care.
Therapy should follow culture and susceptibility results, while catheter replacement removes biofilm that could otherwise serve as a persistent nidus.

question: A 64-year-old intensive care patient with diabetes has an indwelling catheter and receives broad-spectrum antibiotics. A urine culture grows Candida, but the patient has no urinary or systemic symptoms. Which next step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Catheter removal alone resolves candiduria in more than one-third of asymptomatic cases and removes the device associated with colonization.

Fluconazole is first-line therapy for symptomatic Candida cystitis or pyelonephritis and selected high-risk patients. This patient is asymptomatic and has no stated high-risk indication for dissemination.

options.text: Begin antibacterial therapy for seven days
options.rationale: The cultured organism is fungal rather than bacterial, so antibacterial treatment would not target the finding. It would fit a bacterial catheter-associated infection.
The catheter is a modifiable contributor to candiduria. Retention forfeits the intervention that can resolve many asymptomatic cases.
Sulfonamide therapy does not treat Candida candiduria. A change in antibacterial therapy would require a susceptible bacterial infection.

question: A catheterized patient has Candida cystitis with dysuria and urinary frequency. Which treatment is first-line after addressing the catheter?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Cephalexin is an antibacterial drug and is identified as empiric treatment in pregnancy, not therapy for Candida infection.
Nitrofurantoin is used for uncomplicated bacterial cystitis. It is not the stated first-line regimen for symptomatic Candida urinary infection.
Fosfomycin is an empiric option for uncomplicated bacterial cystitis. It would not address symptomatic Candida infection.
Fluconazole reaches high urinary concentrations and is the first-line regimen for symptomatic Candida infections of the urinary tract.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treats selected bacterial urinary infections, not Candida cystitis. It would fit uncomplicated bacterial cystitis when otherwise appropriate.

question: A 10-week pregnant woman has a positive screening urine culture but no urinary or systemic symptoms. Which management is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: No treatment unless urinary symptoms develop
options.rationale: Pregnancy is a specific indication to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria because of increased pyelonephritis, premature-delivery, and low-birth-weight risks.

options.text: Culture-directed oral therapy for five to seven days
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated with a 5-7-day oral course, followed by periodic screening for recurrence.
A 14-day parenteral regimen is used for overt pyelonephritis in pregnancy. This patient has asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Fluoroquinolones should be avoided in pregnancy because of adverse effects on fetal cartilage development. A pregnancy-appropriate oral agent should be selected.

options.text: Sulfonamide therapy throughout the first trimester
options.rationale: Sulfonamides should be avoided in the first trimester because of possible teratogenic effects. Another pregnancy-appropriate culture-directed agent is required.

question: A 30-year-old woman at 27 weeks of gestation has fever, dysuria, and flank pain. Which initial treatment strategy is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Single-dose fosfomycin is an option for uncomplicated cystitis, not overt pyelonephritis during pregnancy.
A short oral cystitis regimen does not match overt pyelonephritis. This presentation requires prompt initial parenteral treatment.
Pregnancy-associated pyelonephritis requires prompt parenteral β-lactam therapy, with a 14-day total treatment course generally sufficient.
Pregnancy-associated pyelonephritis carries a high risk of premature labor and requires prompt empiric therapy rather than observation.
The patient is not in the first trimester, and sulfonamides are not the stated initial regimen for overt pyelonephritis. Parenteral β-lactam therapy is indicated.

question: A 22-year-old pregnant woman has dysuria and frequency without fever or flank pain. Empiric therapy is needed. Which drug is preferred?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Sulfonamides should be avoided in the first trimester and near term because of fetal risks. They would be considered only outside those periods when otherwise appropriate.
Fluoroquinolones should be avoided during pregnancy because of adverse effects on fetal cartilage development.
Amoxicillin was traditionally used, but rising resistance makes it less suitable for empiric selection. It could be used if culture results demonstrated susceptibility.
Ampicillin was traditionally used, but resistance rates have risen. It would be appropriate only if susceptibility data supported its use.
Cephalexin is identified as the drug of choice for empiric treatment of urinary infection during pregnancy.

question: A 76-year-old nursing facility resident has a positive urine culture obtained during routine screening. She has no urinary complaints, fever, leukocytosis, or planned procedure. Which management is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Begin empiric antibiotics to prevent recurrence
options.rationale: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria does not prevent symptomatic infection or recurrent bacteriuria and increases adverse events and resistance.
Treatment often fails to clear bacteriuria, particularly when devices are present, and is not indicated solely to eradicate colonization.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in an older nonpregnant patient without planned mucosa-bleeding urologic surgery should not be treated.
Continuous prophylaxis is a last-line strategy for recurrent symptomatic cystitis, not an intervention for incidental asymptomatic bacteriuria.

options.text: Treat until repeat culture becomes negative
options.rationale: Culture eradication is not a treatment goal in this population because therapy does not reduce symptomatic infection and promotes resistance.

question: A 58-year-old asymptomatic man has bacteriuria and will undergo urologic surgery expected to cause mucosal bleeding. Which next step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Ignore the culture because symptoms are absent
options.rationale: Absence of symptoms usually argues against treatment, but planned urologic surgery with likely mucosal bleeding is a specific exception.

options.text: Delay all management until symptoms appear
options.rationale: Waiting is inappropriate before a qualifying urologic procedure. Treatment is indicated even without symptoms when mucosal bleeding is expected.

options.text: Use prolonged empiric prophylaxis without culture guidance
options.rationale: When asymptomatic bacteriuria requires treatment, the urine culture should direct antimicrobial selection rather than prolonged unguided therapy.

options.text: Treat according to urine culture results
options.rationale: Persons undergoing urologic surgery with likely mucosal bleeding should receive treatment for asymptomatic bacteriuria, directed by culture results.

options.text: Replace treatment with increased water intake
options.rationale: Hydration is a recurrent-UTI prevention measure but does not replace indicated antimicrobial treatment before mucosa-bleeding urologic surgery.

question: A 48-year-old man has dysuria, urgency, fever, chills, myalgias, obstructive voiding symptoms, and a tender swollen prostate. Which treatment is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the spectrum of urinary tract infection (UTIs)

options.text: Oral fluoroquinolone for ten to fourteen days
options.rationale: The systemic symptoms, obstructive complaints, and tender swollen prostate indicate acute prostatitis, treated with an oral fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 10-14 days.
Single-dose fosfomycin is an uncomplicated cystitis regimen. It does not match the longer treatment required for acute prostatitis.

options.text: Nitrofurantoin for five to seven days
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin is used for uncomplicated lower urinary infection. Acute prostatitis requires a 10-14-day fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole course.

options.text: Fluconazole for seven to fourteen days
options.rationale: Fluconazole treats symptomatic Candida urinary infection. The described syndrome is acute bacterial prostatitis caused commonly by gram-negative bacilli.

options.text: Cephalexin for five to seven days
options.rationale: A 5-7-day cephalexin course is associated with pregnancy-related lower urinary treatment, not the stated regimen for acute prostatitis.

question: A 55-year-old man has recurrent infections with symptom-free intervals. His prostate is normal on palpation between episodes. Which treatment duration best matches this condition?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the spectrum of urinary tract infection (UTIs)

options.rationale: Single-dose therapy is used for selected uncomplicated cystitis regimens. Chronic prostatitis requires prolonged treatment.
A 3-day regimen may be used for uncomplicated cystitis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. It is inadequate for chronic prostatitis.
A short course is used for uncomplicated cystitis with agents such as nitrofurantoin. Chronic prostatitis requires substantially longer therapy.
Ten to fourteen days is the initial range for acute prostatitis. Recurrent chronic prostatitis requires a prolonged course.
Chronic prostatitis presents with recurrent infection and may have a normal examination between episodes; fluoroquinolones are generally used for 4-6 weeks or longer.

question: A 67-year-old woman with a cystocele has repeated simple cystitis episodes and increased postvoid residual urine. Which risk-factor category best explains her recurrence?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Frequent intercourse and diaphragm-spermicide use are behavioral risks more typical of younger women. The load-bearing finding here is impaired bladder emptying.
Enhanced coliform adherence is a biologic or genetic risk, but it does not explain the documented residual urine and cystocele.
Cystocele and increased postvoid residual urine are mechanical or physiologic urologic factors that promote recurrence, particularly after menopause.
No immunosuppressive medication or host-defense impairment is provided. Such a factor would require a stated treatment compromising immunity.
No catheter is present, so catheter biofilm cannot explain the recurrences. This category would fit long-term indwelling catheter use.

question: A 24-year-old woman has recurrent cystitis temporally associated with intercourse. She prefers prevention tied only to the triggering event. Which strategy is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.rationale: Continuous prophylaxis exposes the patient every day and is used when other strategies fail. It does not match her preference for event-linked prevention.
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria does not prevent symptomatic recurrence and promotes resistance. It is reserved for pregnancy or qualifying urologic surgery.
An indwelling catheter increases bacteriuria and infection risk. It would be used only for an independent drainage indication.
A single antimicrobial dose after intercourse directly matches recurrences linked to sexual activity and limits exposure compared with continuous prophylaxis.
Postcoital prevention uses a single antibiotic dose, not parenteral treatment. Parenteral therapy is reserved for conditions such as pregnancy-associated pyelonephritis.

question: A hospital quality team wants the single most effective intervention for preventing catheter-associated urinary infection. Which intervention should receive priority?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and management of different types of UTIs (asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated UTIs, UTI in an obstructed urinary tract, and others)

options.text: Remove catheters as soon as possible
options.rationale: Discontinuing catheter use as soon as possible is the most effective preventive measure because catheter duration is the major determinant of bacteriuria.

options.text: Change drainage bags at fixed intervals
options.rationale: Drainage-system maintenance matters, but scheduled bag changes do not address the dominant risk created by continued catheterization.

options.text: Open drainage systems for routine cleaning
options.rationale: A closed drainage system should be maintained. Routine opening increases manipulation and contamination risk.

options.text: Place drainage bags above bladder level
options.rationale: The drainage bag should remain below bladder level. Raising it violates recommended catheter care.

options.text: Treat every episode of catheter bacteriuria
options.rationale: Long-term catheter bacteriuria is expected, and treatment without appropriate clinical indications promotes adverse events and resistance.
